title: Retention chasing service for building subcontractors
oneLiner: RetainRelease tracks every retention balance across every contract, sends the chase letters proven to release the cash, and files construction adjudication if a main contractor refuses.
whoPays: UK subcontracting firms (typically 1-50 staff electricians, plumbers, bricklayers, joiners, groundworkers, plasterers, roofers) working on construction projects where main contractors hold retention. They are paid less per job than main contractors, are squeezed on margin, and have multiple live contracts with held-back cash they rarely chase.
whyNow: The collapse of large main contractors since 2018 (Carillion, Berkeley, ISG, numerous mid-tier firms) has left retention money trapped in insolvent estates, with subbies waiting years for a fraction of what they are owed. The Construction Industry Fairness Charter (2024) and the Procurement Act 2023 are pushing the industry toward audited, faster release. Adjudication is the only statutory route that forces release in 28 days and is enforceable as a court order, so the value of an automated chase-and-adjudicate tool rises as more main contractors use insolvency to delay payment.

premortem.strongestAlternative: A construction solicitor or quantity surveyor, charging £500 to £2,000 per individual chase or adjudication.

adversarial.killCase: Nothing in the passages makes this service unlawful, UK law itself creates the 28-day adjudication route the product uses, no passage compares the cost of winning a customer against what that customer could pay, and no passage shows any single provider holding most of this market (Payapps is named but with no share or customer figures). The one grounded risk is to demand rather than legality: a Commercial Payments Bill introduced in Parliament on 19 May 2026 would ban held-back retention money under construction contracts outright, and if it passes there is eventually no held-back cash left to chase.

The bet
Stated plainly, so you can disagree with it:

UK construction holds between £3bn and £5bn of retention money at any time. When a sub-contractor (electrician, plumber, bricklayer, joiner) sends an invoice, the main contractor typically holds back 3-5% until practical completion and the end of the defects period, usually 12 to 24 months later. The subbie is owed the money but rarely chases it, because the process is admin-heavy and they fear losing future work with the main contractor.

The subbie does have a legal right to release. The Construction Act (Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996, as amended by the Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009) gives them the right to enforce payment through a fast-track 28-day binding decision called adjudication. A court will enforce the adjudicator's ruling, and the adjudicator's decision is binding even if the main contractor disputes it. The catch is that the subbie must follow the contract's exact notice procedure, build the right evidence pack, and file the adjudication correctly. Most subbies do not bother, so the main contractor keeps the cash for free.

RetainRelease does the chasing automatically. The subbie enters each contract (main contractor name, contract value, retention percentage, defects period end date) and the tool tracks the release date for every job. As the date approaches, it sends the contractually-required chase letter with the evidence pack attached: architect's certificate or practical completion statement, snagging list signed off, any contractual notices already served. If the main contractor disputes or simply does not respond within the contractual window, the tool files the 28-day adjudication with a partner construction lawyer who specialises in the route.

The value compounds as enforcement gets more aggressive. Since 2018, the collapse of Carillion, ISG, and dozens of mid-tier main contractors has left retention money trapped in insolvent estates where insolvency practitioners distribute to secured creditors first and subbies last. The government's Construction Industry Fairness Charter (launched 2024) and HMRC's increased scrutiny of retention practices are pushing the industry toward faster, audited release. Adjudication is increasingly the only way to recover retention before the insolvency practitioner distributes assets. The courts and the regulator can publish guidance and run free first-party templates, but they cannot run a commercial retention chaser, cannot take a commercial side against a main contractor, cannot hold the cross-main-contractor dataset that RetainRelease builds, and cannot serve the subbie adversarially to the duty-imposer.

The durable wedge is the proprietary dataset of main contractor retention release behaviour. Each release adds a data point: which main contractors release on time, which dispute, which require adjudication, which pay after the adjudicator's ruling. New subbies use the dataset to choose which main contractors to work for before signing. Insurers and quantity surveyors use it to price credit risk. Late copiers cannot catch up because the data compounds with every contract.
